section_structure.heading: Introduction (untitled)
section_structure.summary: Opens from the Rhetoric 1404a passage where Aristotle pairs lexis with phantasia ('all these things are forms of outward show [phantasia] and intended to affect the audience'). Frames the project: read the Rhetoric alongside De Anima to see that phantasia binds Aristotle's art of rhetoric to his psychology and phenomenology. Three programmatic theses announced: (1) lexis and phantasia together reveal the visual quality of rhetorical style; (2) the lexis-phantasia tie discloses a basic visual component in civic discourse most clearly visible in the epideictic species; (3) consequently there is a 'rhetorical order' in Aristotle's theory of rhetoric in which the epideictic function — marked by imaging and a spatial logic — plays a primal and foundational role. Signposts Quintilian (Inst. Or. 4.2.29, 32) and David Freedberg as anticipations of the visual reading.

section_structure.heading: Phantasia in De Anima
section_structure.summary: Sets out the De Anima account in conversation with Nussbaum (1978/1994), Frede (1992), Schofield (1992), Sorabji (1972), Wedin (1988), Turnbull (1994), White (1985), Caston (1996), and Birondo (2001). Notes that phantasia appears only nine times in the Rhetoric but its cognates pervade it. Endorses Nussbaum's broadening of phantasia beyond 'mental image' to 'what appears,' while insisting (with Schofield) that the visual remains paradigmatic for Aristotle. Phantasia (DA 429a, 428a, 427b, 428b, 431a-b, 432a, 433a-b, 434a) is presented as: integral to all animal psychic life; a movement caused by sense-perception and hence a kind of 'psyche-sight' (etymologically tied to phaos at 429a); essential to the formation of doxa, to deliberative reasoning (bouleutikē, 434a), and to all human action; nevertheless fallible. The crowning analogy 'in phantasian we are like spectators looking at something dreadful or encouraging in a picture' (427b) is mined for its rhetorical implications: phantasia entails spectatorship and distance, an internal theatre.

section_structure.heading: Lexis as Phantasia
section_structure.summary: Reads Rhetoric III.1 (1404a) on the joint signification of lexis and phantasia, taking Kennedy's 'outward show' over Freese's 'mere outward show' as more faithful to Aristotle's non-disparaging usage. Builds two parallels between De Anima phantasia and Rhetoric lexis: (a) form — both are dynamic, visual operations, both turn on dēloi/saphēs/manifestation; pro ommatōn poiein in the Rhetoric (1411b) corresponds to tithēmi pro ommatōn in De Memoria (450a) and Poetics 1455a; both put 'mental images [phantasmata] like objects perceived except that they are without matter' (DA 432a) before the mind's eye; (b) relation to the emotions — lexis is associated with emotional appeals (1404a) and emotions in turn depend on phantasia (DA 427b on the pathos that lies in our power; Rhet. 1382a phobos as phantasia of future evil; 1384a aischynē as phantasia of loss of reputation; 1371a kalon-of-honor via phantasia). Cites Newman (2002) on bringing-before-eyes as a visualizing effect rooted in sense-perception, and on lexis bringing 'a lexical form of energeia, a kind of motion (kinēsis), realized through the capacity of the mind for seeing things in action' (Rhet. 1411b; Metaph. 1048b).

section_structure.heading: Epideictic as visual and primal
section_structure.summary: The centerpiece. Argues that the De Anima ordering of phantasia as a 'lower' or more primal psychic operation — shared with brute beasts, prior to nous, basis for bouleutikē — corresponds to a 'rhetorical order' in which epideictic, as the most overtly lexical species, occupies a primal place. Two-step argument: (a) the basic visual nature of epideictic, and (b) reasons for its primal place. Anchors the visual nature in Rhetoric I.9 amplification (auxesis) — 'amplification, with good reason, falls among forms of praise; for it aims to show superiority' (1368a). The means of amplification are: comparison/analogy (1363b), arguments for relative superiority (1368a), metaphor (1412a), and the lexical devices of expansiveness (1407b), periodos (1409a-b), and pro ommatōn poiein (1411b-1412a). At the center of amplification stands megethos (magnitude/greatness), the Aristotelian root, per Farrell (1995), of megaloprepeia, megalopsychia, and the 'more and the less.' Phantasia provides 'a kind of comparative seeing' (DA 428b; Frede 1992, 286) by which magnitudes can be 'sized up' (sun no bigger than my thumb). The epideictic auditor is named theōros (1358b) — verbal form theōrō, to view, to behold; in De Anima theōrō is repeatedly tied to phantasia (427b). Reads Rosenfeld (1980): the epideictic auditor is a 'witness or seer' who sees with the mind's eye, but corrects Rosenfeld's Heideggerian-contemplative gloss into a phantasia-grounded one. Two functional roles of epideictic discourse then emerge: (1) it shapes the affective ground of deliberation/judgment by activating phantasia-emotion linkages (Fortenbaugh 1975; Nussbaum 1994); (2) it produces the spatial-comparative phantasmata that underlie subsequent practical/pragmatic deliberation. Pericles' Funeral Oration (Thuc. 2.21-22, 2.43) is invoked as the test case: an 'imaginary Athens' (Loraux 1986) — phantasmatic Athens — that grounds collective judgment about magnitude (greatness vs. lesserness).

section_structure.heading: Conclusion
section_structure.summary: Confronts what Lanham calls epideictic's 'classificatory problem' (1991, 164) by recasting epideictic as a discursive function rather than a generic or historical category. Engages Walker (2000) who argues that epideictic is generically/historically primary; O'Gorman shifts the emphasis: 'epideictic's role lay not in shaping presuppositions but in providing common images for a people and shaping their sense of scale.' Re-states the axiom: 'the primal function of public discourse is the phantasmatic.' Aristotle's higher cognitive practices (nous, deliberation) build on rather than suppress phantasia; analogously, deliberative rhetoric builds on epideictic phantasmata. Coda 'An image of Athens' returns to Pericles' Funeral Oration: the oration as 'a virtual hagiography of Athens,' a phantasmatic instantiation of magnification of noble actions, demonstrating how phantasmatic Athens — a sight pitted against abstraction — undergirded subsequent Athenian deliberation about Athens at war.

outline: Cluster 1 (printed 16-17, intro opening): O'Gorman opens from Rhetoric I.1's antistrophos definition but immediately pivots to a 'less discussed yet still important' passage in book 3 (1404a) where lexis and phantasia are conjoined: 'the subject of expression [lexeōs] has some small necessary place in all teaching... all these things are forms of outward show [phantasia] and intended to affect the audience.' This is to be the entry-point for re-reading the Rhetoric alongside De Anima. Phantasia is signaled as 'a tie between [Aristotle's] art of rhetoric and his psychology and phenomenology (anachronistic though these terms are).'

Cluster 2 (printed 17, intro): Marshals David Freedberg (1989) and D. Thomas Benediktson (2000) on the visual-arts/literature parallels that phantasia underwrites; Quintilian's Latin visiones (Inst. Or. 4.2.29) is invoked as a Latin-rhetorical witness to phantasia-as-rhetorical-vision. The Greek term phantasia and its cognates (phantasma, phainesthai, phantasiai) are described as traveling several semantic trajectories — 'imagination,' 'image,' 'impressions,' 'outward show,' 'appearance' — that all bear on rhetoric.

Cluster 3 (printed 18, intro): Three theses programmatically posted: (i) lexis-phantasia reveals the visual quality of rhetorical style; (ii) the lexis-phantasia tie reveals a basic visual component in civic discourse 'most clearly seen in those discourses Aristotle calls epideictic'; (iii) consequently a 'rhetorical order' is implicated, one that qualifies linear-rationalist interpretations of Aristotle's theory. The epideictic function, marked by imaging and a spatial logic, emerges as 'primal and foundational' for public discourse.

Cluster 4 (printed 18-21, S1 Phantasia in De Anima): Surveys the interpretive controversies in DA III.3. Endorses Nussbaum's (1978) corrective to the strict image-theory (Sorabji 1972) — phantasia is the faculty of 'appearances in a broad sense' — but retains the priority of sight that Schofield (1992) and Hett (1935) emphasize. Catalogs De Anima evidence: 427b (phantasia distinct from thought and sense-perception, yet a 'necessary condition for thought to function'); 428a (phantasia is a dunamis/hexis 'by which we judge,' though fallible and most active 'when we do not perceive distinctly'); 428b ('imagination must be a movement produced by sensation actively operating'; etymology from phaos/light at 429a); 429a (phantasia as kind of after-image); 432a (phantasmata 'like aisthemata, only without matter'); 434a (bouleutikē as combining many phantasmata into one). Quotes Frede's tripartite designation: capacity, ongoing appearance, and what appears.

Cluster 5 (printed 22, S1 continued): Pulls out three load-bearing De Anima moves: (i) DA describes deliberation as bouleutikē, a phantasma-combining mental activity; (ii) phantasia is fallible — appearances 'are inherently instable and often unreliable'; (iii) phantasia 'underlies and mediates between sense perception and the mind.' This trio — visual quality, mediating function, epistemic fallibility — is then mapped onto rhetoric: judgment (krisis), whether private or public, 'entails deliberation about appearances.'

Cluster 6 (printed 23-24, S2 Lexis as Phantasia): At the head of S2 sits the lexis/phantasia conjunction at 1404a. Kennedy's 'outward show' is preferred to Freese's 'mere outward show' on the grounds that Aristotle here does not disparage phantasia. Lexis is correlated with saphēs/dēloi/dēlōsai (1404a) — 'to make visible or manifest' — so that style itself becomes a vehicle of pictorial manifestation. Two corroborating axes: form (lexis and DA's phantasia both dynamic, both visual, both image-deploying) and effect (both work on the emotions).

Cluster 7 (printed 24-25, S2 continued): Pro ommatōn poiein in the Rhetoric (1411b) is paired with tithēmi pro ommatōn in De Memoria (450a) and pro ommatōn tithemenon in Poetics (1455a). The Rhetoric's externally directed lexis-imaging and the De Anima's internally directed phantasmatic activity 'mirror each other's form... and power.' Cites Newman (2002, 8-9, 12, 20) on metaphor-prompted visualization, on the rooting of 'bringing before the eyes' in sense-perception, and on the energeia/kinēsis dimension by which lexis activates an audience's phantasmatic capacities (Rhet. 1411b; Metaph. 1048b).

Cluster 8 (printed 25, S2 closing): The effect of lexis on the emotions is grounded in DA 427b's account of pathos as the kind of phantasia 'that lies in our power.' This is then mapped to specific Rhet. passages: 1382a (phobos as phantasia of future destructive or painful evil); 1384a (aischynē as phantasia of loss of reputation); 1371a (kalon/honor through each person's phantasian that he has the qualities of an important person). Speakers thus use lexis to evoke emotion-bearing phantasmata in audiences.

Cluster 9 (printed 26, S2 closing/S3 opening): Reads Rhetoric 1358b (krisis vs. theōria), 1354a (warping the jury by leading them into anger/envy/pity), and 1404a (lexis is artistic, entechnon, hence prone to misuse) — lexis 'is integral to rhetorical judgment, even as it renders rhetorical judgment problematic.' Then introduces epideictic as 'the rhetoric of "showing forth" — the most lexical of the rhetorical species,' and engages Schiappa (1999) who has argued that Aristotle invented his account of epideictic; O'Gorman concedes the historical-generic worry but proposes to recoup the account by reading it as a functional rather than a generic account.

Cluster 10 (printed 27, S3 opening): Maps the De Anima ordering — phantasia as 'lower'/'primal,' shared with beasts, basis for bouleutikē — to a rhetorical ordering in which epideictic is primal. Promises a two-step argument: (a) basic visual nature of epideictic, (b) its primal place in public discourse.

Cluster 11 (printed 27-28, S3 visual nature): Cites Rhetoric 1368a on amplification (auxesis): 'amplification, with good reason, falls among forms of praise; for it aims to show superiority... amplification is most at home in those that are epideictic; for these take up actions that are agreed upon, so that what remains is to clothe the actions with greatness [megethos] and beauty [kallos].' Lists the lexical means of amplification: analogy (1363b), arguments for relative superiority (1368a), metaphor (1412a), expansiveness (1407b), the period (1409a-b), and bringing-before-the-eyes (1411b-1412a).

Cluster 12 (printed 28-29, megethos centerpiece): Megethos is the centerpiece. Quoting Farrell (1995, 186): megethos is 'the root of a great many recurring issues in Aristotelian inquiry,' tied morphologically and conceptually to megaloprepeia, megalopsychia, the 'more and the less,' big and small. Megethos is 'a quality relative to time, place, and circumstance' (Rhet. 1362a-1363a, 1360b, 1362b) that 'addresses the realm of appearances.' DA 428b's 'comparative seeing' (Frede 1992, 286) provides the psychic correlate — appearances can be 'sized up' by comparison and contrast.

Cluster 13 (printed 29-30, theōros): The epideictic auditor at Rhet. 1358b is the theōros — the 'viewer/beholder.' Theōros has a denotational range from 'spectator' (athletic event) to 'philosopher' (contemplative). In DA, theōrō is repeatedly tied to phantasia, especially at 427b ('in imagination we are like spectators looking at something dreadful or encouraging in a picture'). Rosenfeld (1980) is endorsed for connecting epideictic with mind's-eye witnessing, but corrected: not Being-witnessing (Rosenfeld's Heideggerian gloss) but image-witnessing produced through lexis.

Cluster 14 (printed 30-31, S3 primal function): The 'primal' character of epideictic is unfolded. Epideictic 'demotes' the rhetorical species to the foundational level of phantasia-shaped desire/emotion. Sullivan (1992) on rhetoric of belief, Hauser (1999) on common language of values, and Walker (2000) on epideictic priority are gathered as cognate views. O'Gorman aligns with them but shifts the locus from belief to sight and scale.

Cluster 15 (printed 31, S3 two functions): Epideictic discourse functions in two main ways: (1) it shapes the affective ground of deliberation/judgment by drawing on phantasia to engage doxa — emotions arise from phantasia of objects judged true/false (DA 428a-b; Rhet. 1382a, 1384a); (2) it produces phantasmata of magnitude that underlie subsequent practical/pragmatic deliberation (1368a on auxesis; Pericles' Funeral Oration as exemplum).

Cluster 16 (printed 32-33, megalopsychia + EN 1123b): The figure of the megalopsychos (great-souled man) from EN 1123b is invoked: 'megalopsychia, especially in epideictic amplification, is a means by which megalopsychia appears as such in public.' This phantasmatic appearance underlies subsequent pragmatic judgments. The spatial-comparative logics of epideictic 'lay the phenomenological ground of pragmatic rhetorics.' Pericles in the Funeral Oration compares Athens to Sparta and so 'configures for Athenians a sense of their space, of the relative shape and scale of their city.'

Cluster 17 (printed 33, S3 closing): Acknowledges that Aristotelian epideictic does not stand isolated from the other species: 1358b folds it into the temporal triad (past/present/future); 1.3 and 1.9 in tension on whether epideictic is a separate eidos. Reads Lanham's 'classificatory problem' as best resolved by treating epideictic as a function rather than a fixed genre — a function that can be present across deliberative and forensic occasions (Walker 2000, 41).

Cluster 18 (printed 34-35, Conclusion): Re-states the central axiom: 'the primal function of public discourse is the phantasmatic.' Aristotle's higher cognitive practices (nous, deliberation, the virtues) do not suppress phantasia but build on it. Likewise, deliberative rhetoric builds on the corporate phantasmata produced by epideictic. Confronts Schiappa (1999): O'Gorman concedes Aristotle's epideictic may be 'historically inaccurate' as a generic classification, but argues it is best read as a phantasmatic function rather than a generic-historical claim.

Cluster 19 (printed 35-37, Coda: An image of Athens): Reads Pericles' Funeral Oration via Thucydides (2.21-22, 2.43). The Spartan invasion of Attica in 431 BCE is recast as an event of collective sight ('when they saw the army at Acharnae, only seven miles from Athens... their land was being laid waste in front of their very eyes'). The funeral oration is then a 'virtual hagiography of Athens,' the key trope being sight — 'theōmenous every day on the greatness of Athens.' Citing Loraux (1986, 328), Athens here is an 'imaginary Athens,' phantasmatic Athens, configured in a 'spatial logic of greatness' rather than a sequential logic of narrative or theory. This is presented as Aristotle's 'primal role of lexical imaging to political deliberation' in epideictic-styled form.

Cluster 20 (printed 37-40, Notes + Works Cited): Heavy footnote apparatus (23 footnotes). Key footnotes: n.4 (Keuls on the etymological non-identity of energeia and enargeia and their semantic contamination in rhetorical literature); n.5 (Nussbaum 1978 on phantasia/phainesthai); n.6 (Birondo 2001 and Rouveret 1989 on the visual priority); n.10 (Homer as Aristotle's energeia-exemplar at 1411b); n.13 (megalopsychia at EN 1123b); n.17 (Nussbaum 1994 on emotions as not 'irrational'); n.23 (Loraux on the 'imaginary' Athens). Works Cited (selective): Annas 1980, Aristotle (Rhetoric, Poetics, NE, DA, De Memoria, Metaphysics, De Motu Animalium), Benediktson 2000, Birondo 2001, Caston 1996, Chase 1961, Condit 1985, Farrell 1995, Fortenbaugh 1968/1975/1986, Fowler 1989, Frede 1987/1992, Hauser 1999, Havelock 1963, Herodotus, Hett 1935, Isocrates, Kennedy 1991, Keuls 1978, Lanham 1991, Leighton 1982, Lobkowicz 1967, Loraux 1986, McKeon 1947, Newman 2002, Nussbaum 1978/1994, Ong 1982, Quintilian, Rosenfield 1980, Rouveret 1989, Schiappa 1999, Schofield 1992, Sorabji 1972, Striker 1980, Sullivan 1992/1993, Thucydides, Turnbull 1994, Walker 1993/2000, Wedin 1988, White 1985, Wolin 1960.

concepts.label: Phantasia as the proper home of epideictic function
concepts.summary: O'Gorman's signature thesis: phantasia is most rhetorically operative not in Book III's pro ommatōn poiein narrowly construed, but in the epideictic function of discourse, where lexis produces magnitude-bearing phantasmata that underlie subsequent deliberation.

concepts.label: Lexis as phantasia-medium
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1404a's identification of lexis-objects as 'forms of outward show [phantasia]' is read non-disparagingly: lexis is the rhetorical medium that produces phantasmata in the auditor's psyche, paralleling the De Anima account of phantasia as image-producing movement caused by sense-perception.

concepts.label: Megethos as the centerpiece of amplification
concepts.summary: Megethos (magnitude, greatness), per Farrell (1995, 186), is 'the root of a great many recurring issues in Aristotelian inquiry,' tied to megaloprepeia, megalopsychia, the more and less. It sits at the center of amplification (auxesis) in epideictic and is the phantasmatic operation by which scale/superiority is rendered visible.

concepts.label: Bringing before the eyes as lexical kinēsis
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1411b's pro ommatōn poiein is read as a 'lexical form of energeia,' a kinēsis of mind realized through the capacity for seeing-in-action; corresponds to De Memoria's tithēmi pro ommatōn (450a) and Poetics' pro ommatōn tithemenon (1455a).

concepts.label: Rhetorical order paralleling the De Anima psychic order
concepts.summary: Just as in De Anima phantasia is psychically 'lower'/primal yet foundational for higher cognition (nous, deliberation), so epideictic is rhetorically 'primal' yet foundational for deliberative/judicial rhetoric — a 'rhetorical order' that qualifies linear-rationalist readings of the Rhetoric.

concepts.label: Comparative seeing (phantasia and the sizing-up of magnitude)
concepts.summary: Frede's gloss on DA 428b: phantasia provides a 'kind of comparative seeing' by which immediate appearances (sun the size of a thumb) are sized up via comparison/contrast to other objects. This grounds the rhetorical operation of magnitude-construction.

concepts.label: The epideictic auditor as theōros (viewer/beholder)
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1358b's classification of audience-roles names the epideictic auditor theōros rather than kritēs (judge). Theōros bridges spectator/philosopher/contemplator denotations and is repeatedly tied in DA to phantasia (427b's 'spectator at a picture').

concepts.label: Phantasmatic function as primal function of public discourse
concepts.summary: The axiomatic claim: 'the primal function of public discourse is the phantasmatic.' Public deliberation rests on a corporate-phantasmatic nexus of images of scale produced by epideictic discourse.

concepts.label: Phantasia as 'psyche-sight'
concepts.summary: Phantasia is read as a sort of inner sight — etymologically tied to phaos (light) at DA 429a, presented as a 'movement produced by sensation actively operating' (428b); the inner correlate of bodily seeing.

concepts.label: Coupling of phantasia to the emotions in rhetoric
concepts.summary: Rhetorical emotions are themselves definitionally phantasiai: phobos = phantasia of future evil (1382a), aischynē = phantasia of loss of reputation (1384a), kalon/honor via each person's phantasian (1371a). Lexis works on the emotions because lexis works on phantasia.

concepts.label: Bouleutikē as image-combining phantasia
concepts.summary: DA 434a's bouleutikē (deliberative phantasia) is the capacity of combining many phantasmata into one. Aristotle uses bouleutikē also of political deliberation (NE 1141b, Pol. 1329a, Rhet. 1383a). The continuity is significant: rhetorical deliberation is structurally the combination of phantasmata.

concepts.label: Fallibility of phantasia and its rhetorical ambivalence
concepts.summary: Phantasia is 'evidently fallible' (DA 428a) — most active 'when we do not perceive distinctly.' This grounds Aristotle's ambivalence about lexis in Rhetoric III: lexis is necessary but dangerous because it can warp judgment (1354a).

concepts.label: Epideictic's classificatory problem reframed as function
concepts.summary: Lanham's (1991, 164) 'classificatory problem' — epideictic does not fit neatly with deliberative/forensic — is resolved by treating epideictic as a function rather than a genre. Per Walker (2000), epideictic is generically primary; per O'Gorman, it is functionally phantasmatic and underlies the others.

concepts.label: Spatial logic of greatness vs. linear logic of theory/narrative
concepts.summary: Epideictic deploys a spatial logic of combination and comparison (more/less, big/small, near/far) rather than the linear/sequential logic of theory or narrative. This is the phenomenological-rhetorical ground of pragmatic deliberation (Pericles' 'imaginary Athens').

concepts.label: Phantasmatic Athens as paradigm of epideictic image-production
concepts.summary: Pericles' Funeral Oration (Thuc. 2.43) is read with Loraux (1986, 328) as the construction of 'imaginary Athens' — a phantasmatic Athens grounded in a spatial logic of greatness — that subsequently underwrites Athenian pragmatic deliberation in the Peloponnesian War.

concepts.label: Lexis as entechnon — artistic risk in rhetorical judgment
concepts.summary: Rhet. 1404a's characterization of lexis as artistic (entechnon) renders it doubly risky: speakers may serve their whims rather than prudent ends, and lexis-produced phantasmata may corrupt the auditor's psyche (1354a's warping the jury). Phantasia is thus essential yet dangerous.

concepts.label: Visualizing effect rooted in sense-perception
concepts.summary: Following Newman (2002, 12), 'bringing before the eyes' is a 'basic visualizing effect that lies in sense perception' — not a literary device confined to ornament, but a psychological process Aristotle theorizes in De Anima and deploys in the Rhetoric.

readings.label: Epideictic-amplification thesis: phantasia's rhetorical home is the epideictic function, anchored in megethos/amplification, not in Book III lexis narrowly construed
readings.summary: Reorients the contemporary scholarly conversation about phantasia-in-Rhetoric away from the style-only reading (in which phantasia simply names the vividness-effect of pro ommatōn poiein) and toward the epideictic function, where amplification of magnitude (auxesis via megethos, megaloprepeia, megalopsychia, kalon) is the primary rhetorical work of phantasia. Anchored in Rhet. I.3 (audience-types: theōros), I.9 (epideictic praise-blame, auxesis as forms of praise), III.10-11 (metaphor, pro ommatōn poiein) read through De Anima's phantasia.

readings.label: Epideictic-as-function reading: a discursive function, not a generic-historical species
readings.summary: Resolves the Schiappa (1999) / Lanham (1991) 'classificatory problem' by re-categorizing epideictic. Aristotle's genre-classification may be historically inaccurate, but the underlying notion of epideictic as a phantasmatic function of discourse — operative across forensic and deliberative occasions — preserves the analytical insight. Aligns with Walker (2000) on epideictic primacy but shifts the explanans from belief/value to sight/scale.

readings.label: Phantasia as marker of a rhetorical order paralleling Aristotle's psychic order
readings.summary: Phantasia's psychic placement in De Anima — 'lower' than nous, prior to deliberation, shared with brute beasts, yet foundational for all higher cognition — is read as licensing a parallel rhetorical order in which epideictic is structurally 'lower'/'primal' yet foundational. This qualifies the dominant linear-rationalist account of the Rhetoric (deliberative > epideictic) by inverting the foundational priorities.

readings.label: Lexis as visual-medium reading corroborated by the DA account of emotion as phantasia
readings.summary: Rhet. III.1's lexis-phantasia conjunction at 1404a is read as a substantive psychological claim: lexis works because it produces phantasmata, and phantasmata move because they activate the doxa-emotion-judgment circuit theorized in DA III. The Rhetoric's definitional pairing of emotions with phantasiai (phobos = phantasia of future evil, etc.) supplies the textual lock.

greek_terms.summary: Centerpiece term. Per Farrell (1995, 186) the 'root of a great many recurring issues in Aristotelian inquiry.' Tied to megaloprepeia, megalopsychia, the more/less. At the heart of amplification in epideictic; cited at Rhet. 1368a as what 'remains to clothe the actions with' once they are agreed upon.

Central term. Word appears only nine times in the Rhetoric but pervasive via cognates. In DA: a movement of the psyche produced by sense-perception, dependent on sight; in Rhet.: the operation by which lexis affects audiences. O'Gorman insists on the broad 'appearances'-sense over the narrow 'image' or 'mere outward show'.
The product of phantasia. DA 432a: 'like aisthemata, only without matter.' Rhet. operates through the production of corporate phantasmata via lexis.
Rhet. 1411b. Cognate with De Memoria's tithēmi pro ommatōn (450a) and Poetics' pro ommatōn tithemenon (1455a). The signature rhetorical operation by which lexis activates audience phantasia.
The subject of Rhetoric III; conjoined with phantasia at 1404a. Lexis is 'artistic' (entechnon) and thus dangerous (Rhet. 1354a); it produces visual images in the auditor's psyche.

Rhet. III.11. The vividness of metaphor. Per Newman (2002, 20): a kind of kinēsis realized in lexis. Per n.4 (Keuls): not etymologically identical to enargeia but contaminated in rhetorical literature.
Latin: illustratio / evidentia. Quintilian's translation-context. Etymologically distinct from energeia but conflated with it in Greco-Roman rhetorical theory.

Rhet. 1358b: the epideictic auditor is theōros (not kritēs). Verbal theōrō repeatedly tied to phantasia in DA. Pythagorean theōria as 'contemplating beautiful things.' Lexical-conceptual bridge between epideictic and phantasia.

greek_terms.first_use_in_ogorman: p.22, p.27, p.33 (printed); p.5, p.6, p.9 (PDF)
greek_terms.summary: DA 434a: bouleutikē as combining many phantasmata into one. Also used in NE 1141b, Pol. 1329a, Rhet. 1383a of political-council deliberation. NE 1113a: proairesis is bouleutikē orexis. Bridges psychic phantasia to civic deliberation.
Rhet. 1358b: deliberative/judicial audiences are kritai. Krisis as end of rhetoric (Rhet. 1358b). Phantasia conditions krisis because lexis-produced phantasmata mediate audience judgment.
Rhet. 1366b: kalos coupled with virtuous action — dynamis euergetikē. The aesthetic-ethical magnitude rendered visible in epideictic amplification.
Virtue of magnitude — material/lexical expenditure as 'dressing up' the subject. NE 1122a-1125a; tied conceptually to megethos.

Virtue of magnitude internalized — the soul whose visible appearance in public is the proper object of epideictic. NE 1123b. Phantasmatic appearance of the megalopsychos underwrites pragmatic judgment.

Rhet. 1368a. Falls among forms of praise; shows superiority; most at home in epideictic — 'clothing actions with greatness [megethos] and beauty [kallos].' The signature operation of epideictic phantasia.
DA 428a: phantasia produces doxa 'exactly corresponding to direct perception.' Per Fortenbaugh: doxa is the efficient cause of emotion. The doxa-phantasia-emotion circuit is what lexis mobilizes.
DA 429a etymology: phantasia derived from phaos because 'without light it is impossible to see.' Emphanizōn (1367b) and dēloi (1404a) form a vocabulary cluster of lexis-as-illumination.
Rhet. 1404a couples lexis with saphēs — clarity as the virtue (aretē) of lexis. Overlaps with dēloi/dēlōsai semantic domain of visual manifestation.
DA 427b: pathos as the kind of phantasia that lies in our power. Rhetorical emotions (phobos, aischynē) defined as phantasiai. The interface between phantasia, doxa, and rhetorical effect.
Rhet. 1367b: praise as the speech that 'makes clear' (emphanizōn) the greatness of virtue. Cognate with phaos/phainesthai — epideictic as illumination.

DA 428b/429a: phantasia is a kinēsis caused by sense-perception. Per Newman: 'bringing before the eyes' is a 'lexical form of energeia, a kind of motion realized through the capacity of the mind for seeing things in action.'
Verbal stem to which phantasia is grammatically related. Nussbaum's broadening of phantasia is via the phainesthai-stem — what appears, not just what is imaged.

tensions.label: Lexis as necessary yet dangerous to rhetorical judgment
tensions.summary: Aristotle at 1404a admits lexis as having a 'small necessary place' but immediately ranks it with phantasia/outward show; at 1354a he warns that lexis can 'warp the jury by leading them into anger or envy or pity.' Phantasia underlies both the necessity (it activates judgment) and the danger (it can corrupt judgment via false phantasmata). O'Gorman reads this ambivalence as itself evidence for the phantasmatic function — Aristotle's anxiety mirrors his recognition of phantasia's psychic power.

tensions.label: Epideictic as historical genre vs. discursive function
tensions.summary: Schiappa (1999) argues Aristotle 'invented' epideictic and his account is historically inaccurate and generically inadequate. Lanham (1991, 164) speaks of epideictic's 'classificatory problem.' Walker (2000) salvages epideictic as generically primary. O'Gorman resolves the tension by treating epideictic as a function (the phantasmatic function of public discourse), which can be operative in deliberative and forensic occasions alike.

tensions.label: Phantasia's 'lowness' in psyche vs. epideictic's 'primality' in rhetoric
tensions.summary: Phantasia is 'lower' in the psyche (shared with brute beasts, prior to nous) yet O'Gorman calls epideictic 'primal' — a positive metaphysical claim about foundationality. The tension is that what is psychically 'lower' becomes rhetorically 'foundational.' O'Gorman exploits this paradox: lowness in the hierarchy of cognition = priority in the order of foundations.

tensions.label: Phantasia as image-faculty (Sorabji) vs. faculty of appearances (Nussbaum)
tensions.summary: The interpretive controversy in De Anima scholarship — does phantasia produce/inspect mental pictures (Sorabji 1972, Wedin 1988) or is it the broader faculty of phainomena (Nussbaum 1978, Schofield 1992)? O'Gorman sides with Nussbaum-Schofield but retains the visual priority that Sorabji emphasizes — phantasia is broader than picturing but sight remains the paradigmatic exercise.

tensions.label: Contemplative theōros (Rosenfield) vs. phantasmatic theōros (O'Gorman)
tensions.summary: Rosenfield (1980) reads the epideictic theōros as a witness to Being — a Heideggerian-contemplative gloss. O'Gorman retains the witness-language but recasts the object: theōros witnesses lexis-produced phantasmata, not Being. The tension: same Greek term, two metaphysical underwritings.

nussbaum_comparison: Where Nussbaum (PHX-01) rescues phantasia from the De Anima III.3 'decaying-sense' enclosure to vindicate it as the faculty of phainomena that underwrites all action-explanation, O'Gorman extends Nussbaum's broadening into the Rhetoric and argues that what phantasia underwrites in civic discourse is specifically the epideictic function. The two papers share (a) the corrective move against Sorabji's image-theory, (b) the privileging of the phainesthai-stem ('what appears') over the narrow image-having, and (c) the appeal to phantasia's role in mediating perception and judgment via emotion/desire. They differ in disciplinary register and load-bearing texts: Nussbaum is a classicist/philosopher mining MA + DA + EN + EE for an action-theoretic account; O'Gorman is a rhetorician mining Rhet. I.3/I.9/III.1-11 + DA + De Memoria + Poetics for an account of rhetorical function. O'Gorman's signature addition is that the lexis-phantasia conjunction at Rhet. 1404a is not a marginal stylistic remark but the textual lock between Aristotle's psychology and his rhetorical theory — and that the epideictic species (Rhet. I.9, amplification via megethos) is the rhetorical equivalent of phantasia's psychic primality in DA III. Nussbaum is cited approvingly at p.19 (printed) on phantasia as 'faculty of appearances in a broad sense' and again at n.5, n.17 on the emotions. The two papers are thus methodologically aligned and substantively complementary: Nussbaum's 'what appears' is the philosophical claim; O'Gorman's 'corporate phantasmata of magnitude' is its rhetorical application.
